problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.

activity_context.topic_title: Finding the Canonical Form of a Quadratic Form Using Orthogonal Transformations

examples.knowledge_point: Reducing a Quadratic Function Over the 2D-Space to the Canonical Form Using Orthogonal Transformations
examples.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=2x_1^2-2x_1x_2+2x_2^2,$ find its canonical (diagonal) form $\mathbf{y}^T \! D \mathbf{y}$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $\mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
examples.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/69dcf821f3ff202b567b901d8f512c5cecf7159617ca51a0664c14a5099e9715.png)

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -1 \\ -1 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +3 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For $\lambda_1=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/fc9465d4e5bcd43a3c29e5946b05ec18cdbc7453a4011aa548f374016c561b45.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/59c1bd46325fab8a52fed162d7ae47e8fb33a10cc524cd770a3b18f5934e51dd.png)

- For $\lambda_2=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/adc9241219f3b5ebce0d8418bf34e250b7230ea612fabca5bdfc109c98a18dbb.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2  \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/dcab437eb77b29ab5bcd5c3ae14b77f10f01382aafadf2aecded1bb1fb72dc32.png)

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076285/assets/3f6b1002893290dde6c9a68425b0035e249ff3630a41d29c9da5756c1a18f6a6.png)

feedback.problem: Using the method of orthogonal transformations, find the canonical form of $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}-{x}_{3}^{2}-6{x}_{1}{x}_{2}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -3 \\ -3 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-9) & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -8) & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )(\lambda -4)(\lambda +2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,-1,\,-2\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, writing the eigenvalues in descending order, we obtain the diagonal matrix

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

The corresponding quadratic form after a change of variables is

$$
4{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}-2{y}_{3}^{2}.
$$
